**Initial Funeral Experience** 
*(Note: The very first human corpse I ever encountered was caught in German barbed wire, where it was impossible to give it a burial.)*

A stench pervaded the entire meadow, and we detected the odor of a dead hound prior to actually seeing it. Its inflated stomach appeared on the verge of exploding. The animal had matted, unkempt fur and empty eye sockets, and a multitude of flies hovered around it on that Good Friday. 

The sight made me feel nauseous and struck me with an intense, icy chill. However, because Rose was the older sibling, she had the bravery to prod the carcass with a twig. The body felt unpleasantly squishy, and as insects buzzed around its head and settled on its brow, Rose softly remarked that the animal had indeed passed away.

She noted that when humans are truly dead, they are buried in the yards surrounding churches with spires, proposing that we should perform a similar burial for this creature. To mask the terrible odor, she suggested surrounding the body with mint. I went searching and discovered a plentiful patch of the herb growing near the water well.

outputs.L3:
On the quiet, heavy afternoon of Good Friday, Rose and I stumbled upon the carcass in the high grass near the edge of the woods. It was a dog, swollen beneath the unseasonably warm sun, its dark fur hidden beneath an iridescent, buzzing cloud of flies. 

The sight made my stomach churn. The awful stench of decay hit the back of my throat, and I stepped back, paralyzed by a mixture of nausea and child-like terror. Rose, who was older and rarely frightened by anything, did not shrink away. Instead, she snapped a sturdy birch branch from a nearby bush and stepped toward the writhing cloud. With a calm, clinical curiosity, she prodded the dog’s bloated side with the stick. The flies scattered with a sharp, angry buzz before settling right back down. 

"Yep," Rose declared, leaning on her stick. "It's completely dead."

Looking up at the gray sky, Rose seemed struck by the gravity of the day. It was Good Friday, after all—a time of mourning and solemn remembrance. She decided it wasn't right to leave the poor creature to rot in the open like trash. With absolute conviction, she announced that we were going to give the dog a proper funeral, just like the ones held for people at the village church.

However, the sheer foulness of the odor made approaching the corpse almost impossible. Remembering the surroundings, Rose sent me to the old stone well at the edge of the clearing. There, fed by the well's damp overflow, grew a thick patch of wild mint. I knelt in the mud and ripped up handfuls of the vibrant green plant, bruising the leaves in my fists until my hands were stained and heavy with the sharp, sweet fragrance. 

Armed with the fresh mint to mask the smell of death, we set to work. Using thick limbs as levers, we grunted and strained until we managed to push the heavy body down into a nearby ditch. I scattered the crushed mint over the dog, painting the dreary scene with bright green leaves, before we both began shoveling loose earth and heavy clay over the body using our hands and makeshift wooden spades. 

When the dog was entirely covered beneath a fresh mound of dirt and aromatic leaves, the foul odor was finally replaced by the scent of crushed mint and damp earth. Rose and I stood side by side at the edge of the grave, folded our hands, and bowed our heads. There, in the quiet shadows of Good Friday, we whispered a solemn final prayer, granting the nameless dog the peace it deserved.
outputs.L4:
The summer of my ninth year was long, dry, and smelled of scorched clover, until the afternoon we crossed the ridge into the un-mown pasture behind the ruined barn. 

My brother Tommy was seven, his shins mapped with old scars and green grass stains. We were hunting for grasshoppers when the air changed. It didn’t arrive as a breeze, but as a wall—a thick, warm weight that coated the back of the throat with the sickly sweet tang of iron and rot. 

We found the source at the edge of the ditch: a hound, once yellow, now swollen and blackened by days beneath the relentless sun. Its hide was tight to bursting, glistening with an iridescent storm of green-bottle flies, and its exposed teeth grinned in a terrible, silent agony. It was the first time either of us had seen physical death—not as a quiet sleeping figure in a casket, but as a violent, grotesque dismantling of life. 

We froze, paralyzed by a mixture of terror and dark fascination. The dog’s eyes were gone, replaced by hollows of busy, pale movement. The sight threatened to shatter the fragile, sunlit world we inhabited. Yet, after the initial shock receded, a strange, quiet necessity took hold of us. It felt impossible to simply walk away and leave this creature to dissolve into nothingness under the scorching sky. 

Tommy began to cry, small silent tears cutting tracks through the dust on his cheeks. "We have to fix it," he whispered.

We could not bring ourselves to touch it with our bare hands. Instead, we gathered long, sturdy branches of fallen oak. Working together, gagging against the waves of foul air, we used the sticks as levers, carefully nudging and rolling the heavy, decaying mass until it tumbled with a wet thud into a deep wash-out hole at the bottom of the ditch. 

The fall disturbed the stench, releasing a cloud of decay so potent it forced us back to the edge of the field, gasping for breath. That was when I noticed the wild spearmint growing thick near the creek bed. 

"Get the mint!" I yelled to Tommy.

We fell upon the patch like desperate gardeners, tearing up armfuls of the green stalk, crushing the leaves between our palms until our hands were stained dark and wet. We ran back to the pit and rained the crushed mint down onto the dog. Green leaves covered the black fur; the sharp, cool scent of menthol fought courageously against the thick perfume of mortality. 

When the dog was completely hidden beneath a blanket of bruised green, we used flat stones and our hands to scrape dry, dusty topsoil into the hole. We worked frantically, throwing dirt until the pit was leveled, until the flies lost their way, until the smell was entirely consumed by the damp scent of freshly turned earth and crushed mint.

When it was done, we stood over the makeshift grave, barefoot and exhausted. Tommy wiped his nose with the back of a dirty hand. 

"Should we say something?" he asked.

I took his hand. "Lord," I said, my voice trembling only slightly, "bless this good dog. Keep him safe in the dark. Amen."

"Amen," Tommy repeated. 

In that small, naive ceremony, we had tamed the monster. We had taken the horrific, raw reality of non-being and softened it with ritual, order, and respect. We walked home in the dusk, believing that death was something that could always be cured with a little dignity, some earth, and sweet herbs.

I carried that comfort for thirty years, until I found myself standing in the gray, frozen mud of a nameless valley half a world away. 

There, beneath a steel sky, lay the casualties of a war that had abandoned all pretenses of mercy. They were not buried. They lay where they had fallen in the trampled snow, stripped of their names, their limbs twisted, their faces exposed to the freezing rain and the black, hungry crows. There were no sticks to gently nudge them into the earth. There were no armfuls of wild mint to mask the heavy, metallic stench of spilled life. There were no children to hold hands and whisper prayers over their quiet forms. 

Standing in the quiet ruin of that adult landscape, watching the frost settle on the hollow eyes of unburied men, I smelled—for just a phantom second—the sharp, sweet scent of crushed summer mint, and felt the devastating weight of a world that had forgotten the simple, merciful grace of two children in a field.
outputs.L5:
**The First Funeral**

Childhood is defined by a quiet assumption of permanence. The trees will always cast the same shadows across the lawn, summer days will stretch out endlessly, and the adults in our lives will always know how to keep the world turning. But for everyone, there comes a moment when that comfortable fiction shatters, marked irrevocably by **the first funeral**.

Before that day, death is an abstract concept—a plot point in a book, a quiet absence spoken of in low tones, or something that happens only to the very old or the distant. But to step into the hushed, heavy atmosphere of a funeral home is to watch abstraction turn brutally real.

The memory of **the first funeral** is rarely built on the words spoken during the eulogy. Instead, it is made of sensory fragments that imprint themselves deep into the mind. It is the suffocating, sweet scent of too many lilies packed into a single room. It is the scratchy discomfort of unaccustomed black clothes and stiff shoes that pinch at the heels. It is the eerie, muffled quality of the air, where every whisper feels magnified and every footstep carries a heavy weight.

For a young person, the most unsettling part of **the first funeral** is often not the casket itself, but the adults. To see a parent weep openly, or to watch a grandparent—the pillar of the family—stand frail and trembling, is a profound shock. It is the moment the protective armor of adulthood falls away, revealing that even the grown-ups are small and vulnerable against the vastness of loss. 

Standing beside the open grave, listening to the dull sound of earth hitting polished wood, something shifts internally. The illusion of personal immortality quietly dissolves. You realize, perhaps for the very first time, that the people you love will not be here forever—and neither will you.

Yet, in a strange way, **the first funeral** is also an initiation into the shared human experience. It teaches us why we gather in the dark valleys of grief: not to undo the loss, but to ensure no one carries it alone. We walk away from that first grave a little older and a little heavier, but with a new, sharp awareness of how precious every ordinary, sunlit day truly is.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled "I. – THE FIRST FUNERAL" with the subtitle "(The first corpse I saw was on the German wires, and couldn’t be buried)". Have a naive young child narrate the memory of finding a dead, bloated dog with their older sister Rose on Good Friday, poking it, and burying it with mint to hide the smell.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. – THE FIRST FUNERAL**  
*(The first corpse I saw was on the German wires, and couldn’t be buried)*

The sun had turned the ditches bright on Good Friday morn,  
When Rose and I went wandering down by the water-mill.  
The church bells chimed for Jesus, far away and slow,  
While all the sleeping village held its breath and kept quite still.  

We found him by the brambles where the wild nettles grow,  
A farmer’s dog, or stray one, lying heavy on his side.  
His belly was a balloon of skin, tight and round and strange,  
As if he’d drunk the morning air and held it till he died.  

I poked him with a hazel twig to see if he would wake,  
His coat felt hard as turnip, his jaw was stiff as stone.  
Rose pulled me by the collar and she knocked my stick away,  
And whispered that we mustn't leave him sitting all alone.  

A thick and sour sweetness started rising from his fur,  
Like apples left to rot beneath the heavy summer rain.  
So Rose ran to the ditch-side where the green mint grew wild,  
And tore up leafy handfuls till her fingers bore the stain.  

We scraped a shallow cradle with a rusty garden trowel  
Beneath the quiet shadows where the elder branches bend.  
We packed the bruised mint leaves all around his swollen ribs,  
To hide the dark and heavy smell and make the bad air mend.  

We smoothed the cool dirt over him and set a little stone,  
And Rose said a short prayer for a dog without a name.  
I thought that every broken thing was gathered up like that—  
Tucked safe into the heavy earth, and buried just the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an eerie, vintage-sounding rhyming poem from a young child's perspective about encountering death for the first time? Make it dark yet innocent, featuring two siblings who give a bloated, decomposing dog a proper Christian burial in a field.
counterfactuals.output:
Sister Mary held my hand,
Past the orchard, wet and grey,
Deep into the clover land,
At the fading of the day.
There we found a noble hound,
Sprawled upon the mossy green,
Tight and round above the ground,
The queerest thing we’d ever seen.

His belly was a leather ball,
His legs were stiff as walking sticks,
He wouldn't answer Mary’s call,
Nor play his usual fetching tricks.
A coat of shiny emerald flies
Was buzzing soft above his head;
He stared right up with glassy eyes,
And Mary whispered, "He is dead."

I asked her what it meant to die,
She said it means the breath goes out,
To wander in the quiet sky,
While coldness wraps the skin about.
"He needs a house," my sister said,
"Before the crows begin to sing,
A proper place to rest his head,
Fit for a servant of the King."

We dug a hole with rusted spoons
Beneath the crooked elderberry,
While crickets hummed their evening tunes
To make our solemn labor merry.
We rolled his heavy, bloated side
Into the dark and waiting clay,
And tucked his tail so neat inside,
And wiped the silver film away.

We bound two twigs of fallen oak
With ribbon from my bonnet lace,
And wrapped him in my woollen cloak
To hide his poor, decaying face.
We folded down his stiffened paws,
And sang a verse of *Rock of Ages*,
To save him from the Devil's jaws,
Like holy men in Sunday pages.

We asked the Lord his soul to keep,
And prayed the rain would wash him clean,
Then left him to his heavy sleep
Deep down beneath the clover green.
My fingers smelled of bitter rust,
And sweet, sour air I could not name—
We left the hound to turn to dust,
Just as the kitchen candles came.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern classic poem in the style of a World War I soldier recalling his very first encounter with death as a child. Use a simple ABAB rhyme scheme and simple language to contrast childish innocence with morbid reality.
counterfactuals.output:
I found a thrush behind the shed
When I was only seven years,
Its tiny eyes were dry and red,
It did not seem to mind my tears.

I touched the wing of speckled grey,
And wondered why it would not fly,
The sun was hot that summer day,
I did not know that things could die.

I built a bed of moss and stone,
To keep it safe against the night,
And left the little bird alone,
And waited for the morning light.

I brought a leaf to shade its head,
I called to it beneath the sun,
My mother said the bird was dead,
And told me that its life was done.

Now here in mud and heavy rain,
Where men fall down and do not rise,
I see that look come back again,
Behind a dying comrade’s eyes.

I cried three days for that small bird,
And hid it gently by the tree,
Now death is just a common word,
And no one weeps for them or me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poem that includes these specific details: a dead dog in a field on Good Friday, flies, a sister named Rose poking it with a stick, planting mint around the grave to cover the smell, and throwing brown dirt over it while saying "Amen!"
counterfactuals.output:
On Good Friday, the sky hung pale and still,
And down in the pasture below the hill,
We found him stretched in the tangled weeds—
A quiet end to his simple needs.
Above his body, the sun shone dim,
As a iridescent swarm of flies hummed over him.

My sister Rose stepped close to the place,
A solemn shadow across her face.
She picked up a fallen birch-wood stick
And poked his side, to see if a kick
Or a twitch of his tail might wake him yet,
Or if his stillness was fully set.

We dug out a grave where the shadow stays,
To keep him safe through the coming days.
And to smother the heavy, rising smell,
We gathered the wild mint growing well
Along the creek, and planted the green
In a fragrant ring where the mound was seen.

Then Rose took a handful of brown dirt, deep
And dark as the soil where the roots all sleep.
She threw the earth down to cover his side,
Where the mint leaves wafted their herbal tide,
And as the last heavy clod was thrown,
She cried to the silent field, "Amen!"
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, simple ballad about childhood innocence confronted by decay.
counterfactuals.output:
Young Clara wore a ribbon white,
And skipped along the lane;
Her laughter caught the morning sun,
Unused to grief or pain.

She wandered past the iron gate
Where wild roses used to grow,
And down into the hollowed woods
Where darker waters flow.

She found an ancient orchard tree
Whose boughs were thick with rust,
Where every apple, black and soft,
Was turning into dust.

Beneath the roots a songbird lay,
Its small eye dull as glass;
A veil of rot had claimed its wings
And tied them to the grass.

She reached to stroke the quiet head,
To wake it from its sleep,
And felt the cold that lives below
Where shadows crawl and creep.

The white silk ribbon in her hair
Was stained a heavy grey;
The sweetness left the summer air
And chased the sun away.

Now Clara walks with silent steps,
Her golden laughter gone;
She knows the mold beneath the flower,
The night inside the dawn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
